_comment: Publish-console 'App config' template (deployment defaults, becomes ENCLAVE_CONFIG via configCid). 'volumes' names the attested model volumes the platform attaches (the wasm-manager mounts each at /models/<name> in the guest - no paths here by design). The 'models' catalog is stated in FULL for all four ggml volumes; the retired onnx volume qwen2.5-0.5b is gone from the gpu fleet so its entry is dropped here (the catalog embedded in the wasm keeps it for local dev). qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf sets tokenizer_file to null EXPLICITLY: ENCLAVE_CONFIG merges per FIELD into the embedded catalog, whose entry still points tokenizer_file at the retired onnx volume - omitting the key would keep that stale cross-volume path, null clears it so the re-wrapped volume's own bundled tokenizer.json serves. 122b/9b geometry from the volumes' GGUF headers (qwen35moe/qwen35) + the shared Qwen3.5 tokenizer; both open replies with a <think> block, which the large max_new budgets and rep_penalty 1 (penalties distort long reasoning) are sized for. With rep_penalty at 1 the only things standing between a reasoning model and a degenerate loop are top_k and the repeat_guard, so BOTH are set on every thinking entry: top_k 40 because measurement on the fable 27b ("write a haiku", 1200 tokens) put repeated 10-grams at 36.3% with top_k off and 10.6% at 40, while temperature barely moved it; and repeat_guard 4, a HARD stop that ends a reply once one identical block of tokens has repeated four times. The guard is the one that actually bounds the damage: think_budget only arms inside a force-opened <think> block, so a model reasoning in plain prose (fable does exactly this with thinking off) had no limit at all short of max_new_cap - observed 2026-07-29 as an 80k-token haiku repeating one line. kv_layers counts only the FULL-ATTENTION layers (hybrid models keep no KV in the linear-attention ones) so the app's VRAM pricing - weights + KV at the NODE's window (llama.cpp allocates the whole ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX up front, not the app's prompt budget) + ~1.5 GB working set - is honest. The 122b needs >=~50% GPU share; the qwen3.6-27b (arch qwen35 in the GGUF, same hybrid SSM family, kv_layers 16 of 64) needs ~28 GB (17.6 weights + 9.1 KV at the 256K node window + working set) = gpu 0.21; the 9b needs ~12 GB (5.6 weights + 4.3 KV at the 256K node window + working set) = gpu 0.09; under that the app now refuses it cleanly instead of the tenant dying by CUDA OOM mid-compute. qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf runs its full native window (32k = 24576 prompt + 8192 gen cap; the embedded 3072 was sized for the retired onnx guest-memory path - ggml KV lives host-side, and the node's ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX 262144 already covers it). think_budget 16384 is set on every thinking model, half of default_max_new: a model that gets stuck in its <think> block re-deriving the same step would otherwise spend the whole 32768-token budget reasoning and answer nothing, so at 16384 the server closes the block itself and the model writes its answer with the remaining half. It is a runaway guard, not a style knob - raise it for work that legitimately reasons longer, drop the key (or 0) to let a model think until max_new. qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf does not reason, so it has none. The fable-fusion 27b ships in TWO quants and 'volumes' attaches the Q4 one, deliberately: both entries describe the same model and geometry, but the Q4 is the one sized for a small share. At the fleet's 176K q8_0 node window (ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX 180224) Q4_K_M costs ~26.8 GB to serve (18.5 weights + 6.7 KV including the lazily-created MTP head context + working set) and Q5_K_M ~29.5 GB, against the 35.1 GB a 25% H200 share holds. That margin was not always there: at the old 256K window the Q5 needed ~32.5 GB, and because the MTP head context is created LAZILY on the first speculative session the deployment served, answered /warmup in 100 ms, and then stalled the first real chat request when the head's KV and buffers exhausted what was left (deployment a025ed60, 2026-07-28). Never attach both fable volumes at once: two 27b preloads is ~40 GB of weights before a byte of KV, and the default pick is the largest attached model that fits. Largest attached model serves as the default.
_search_comment: WEB SEARCH is OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'search' object to turn it on. Absent means the app never makes an outbound request and the playground hides the control entirely. When present, the playground still starts OFF - people choose an enclave because the conversation does not leave it, so reaching outside is always the user's deliberate act, never a default they inherit. The switch (in the model menu) offers off / auto / always. On 'auto' a SHORT router generation asks the MODEL whether the question needs the web, so 'what changed in Rust 1.90' searches and 'rewrite that shorter' does not - which is how a chat app is expected to behave, and it costs one extra tiny generation per turn. web_search:true still searches unconditionally (the 'always' setting), a message beginning '/search ' forces one, and absent never searches. Either way the APP fetches results over wasi:http before building the prompt - from the deployment's own dedicated egress identity, so the user's question goes to the provider from this enclave rather than from their browser. Be honest about what that costs: the provider learns the query and this deployment's IP, and any page the app fetches learns the IP. It does not learn who asked or anything else in the conversation. PICK THE PROVIDER FOR THE NETWORK, FIRST: a deployment's outbound egress leaves from its own dedicated IPv6 and is IPv6-ONLY, so a provider whose host publishes no AAAA record CANNOT be reached and every query dies as ErrorCode::ConnectionRefused. Measured against a live deployment 2026-07-29: api.exa.ai and serpapi.com connect; api.search.brave.com, google.serper.dev and html.duckduckgo.com are refused. So BRAVE, SERPER, TAVILY, BING AND THE KEYLESS 'ddg' DEFAULT ALL FAIL HERE regardless of the key - use 'exa' (or a searxng instance with IPv6). Check any candidate with `dig AAAA <host>` before wiring it. The same constraint hits fetch_pages, which dials each RESULT site directly: most of the web is IPv4-only, so those fetches fail one by one and the hit keeps only its snippet - which is the other reason to prefer exa, whose results carry page text inline (one round trip, and Exa's own network does the fetching). Fields: provider 'exa'|'searxng'|'brave'|'serper'|'ddg' (default ddg, which is IPv4-only - set this explicitly); endpoint (provider base URL override; REQUIRED for searxng); api_key (the credential - set it through SEALED SECRETS, never here, because the configCid is public on-chain); max_results (default 5); fetch_pages (how many top hits to fetch and read in full, default 0 = snippets only - each one is a serial round trip on the request's critical path, so 2 is the usual sweet spot and 5 is slow); page_chars (text kept per fetched page, default 6000, roughly 1.5k tokens); timeout_s (default 15, applied to connect and first byte). Note on 'ddg': it needs no key, which is why it is the default, but it is HTML scraping and DuckDuckGo rate-limits datacentre egress - a deployment that leans on it will start seeing 'duckduckgo declined the query (HTTP 202)'. Anything load-bearing wants brave/serper with a key, or your own searxng (which can itself run in an enclave, leaving no commercial provider in the path). WIRING A KEY, exactly: (1) get the credential from the provider (exa.ai/api - dual-stack, so it is the one that works from here); (2) put the VALUE in the deployment's SECRETS in the console - they are stored on the relay, off-chain, and injected as env vars at every start; never type the key into this file, which is published on-chain by CID and world-readable (the scripted equivalent is set_secrets with payload {"set":{"EXA_API_KEY":"<key>"}}); (3) reference it BY NAME here, e.g. "search": { "provider": "exa", "api_key": "$EXA_API_KEY", "max_results": 5, "fetch_pages": 2 } - the platform substitutes $NAME/${NAME} in config STRINGS from those secrets at launch, so what goes on-chain is the NAME and never the key; (4) restart the deployment, because config and secrets are both read at start. If the secret is missing the placeholder stays a literal, and the app says so by name instead of posting the string "$BRAVE_API_KEY" to Brave and showing you Brave's 401. Verify a live deployment with GET /search?q=test (provider leg) and GET /search?url=https://example.com (fetch+extract leg); the two fail separately and the probe says which. Both are behind the api_key gate when the deployment sets one - ?url= fetches arbitrary URLs from this deployment's egress identity, so it is not left open where an operator asked for auth.
_image_comment: IMAGE GENERATION is OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'image' object pointing at an image-generator deployment and the SAME router that decides about web search will also decide about pictures (only once the user turns the switch on - it starts off) - "draw me a fox" generates one, "what is impressionism" does not. A message beginning '/image ' (or /img, /draw) forces one and skips the router. Absent means the app never calls an image service AND the model is never told the capability exists, so it cannot promise a picture it has no way to make. Fields: endpoint (REQUIRED - the image-generator's base URL, e.g. "https://<id8>.app.enclave.host"; a full /v1/images/generations path is accepted too); api_key (Bearer, when that deployment sets one - reference a SECRET by name, "$IMAGE_API_KEY", never the literal, because this file goes on-chain); model (a name from the image service's catalog, absent = its default, the largest attached); size (default "1024x1024", snapped to the service's limits); timeout_s (default 180 - a 20B MMDiT at 8 steps on a shared H200 is tens of seconds and queues behind other tenants, so this is the one timeout measured in minutes); max_bytes (default 12 MB, the cap on the response - a PNG comes back base64'd at ~1.4x, and exceeding this is reported honestly rather than handing the browser a truncated image). CONTRACT: POST {endpoint}/v1/images/generations with {prompt, n:1, size, model?} -> {data:[{b64_json, seed?}]}, which is exactly what the sibling image-generator app serves. REACHABILITY: outbound egress is IPv6-only, but an image-generator running as another Enclave deployment is fine - every deployment gets a dedicated IPv6. The bytes come back to the browser INLINE as a data: URI, so the picture never costs the user a request to a second origin and a saved chat still renders offline; the cost is carrying it through the SSE stream and into IndexedDB. The text model never sees the image - it is told one was generated and from what prompt, which is enough to acknowledge it without inventing a description.
